newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says EMU needs better securities settlement.
newsitem.headline: EMI says EMU needs better securities settlement.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute said on Thursday European states must take action now to improve their securities settlement systems to pave the way for a joint monetary policy under a common currency.

The forerunner to the European Central Bank said in a report that securities systems had to be made more homogeneous to allow a smoother transfer of securities within the euro area to ensure that banks could gain easy access to central bank lending.
Problems with such systems could undermine monetary policy under a single currency by limiting the responsiveness of the banking system to the centrally-conducted monetary policy.

"This report has been prepared by the Working Group on EU Payment Systems in close co-ordination with monetary policy and legal experts to ensure that payment systems arrangements will be operationally sound and responsive to the needs of the single policy," the EMI report said.

At issue is the need to ensure that banks which need to gain access to central bank liquidity through the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) are able to make a deposit of securities with the central banking system as collateral against a loan. Such collateral will be needed both for longer-term money market operations -- such as securities repurchase tenders -- and also for the provision of temporary intra-day liquidity which ensures no bottlenecks arise in gross payment systems.
The smooth running of such operations is important both to allow monetary policy moves to feed quickly into markets and to ensure the efficient running of the banking system.

The report focused on immediate changes which would have to be in place by the start of "Stage Three" of EMU -- the launch of the single currency in 1999 -- but added that this would only be a starting point, and more integration would be needed.

"Given the time constraints and the long lead times required for possible changes to existing infrastructures, it is important to distinguish between the basic requirements of the single monetary policy and of payment systems at the start of Stage Three, the preparation of which is imperative before the start of Stage Three, and further requirements which may not be fulfilled at the start of EMU," the report said.
Although all EU countries already had functioning settlement systems, these systems varied greatly, the EMI said.
"Major differences exist concerning the following: participants in the systems, settlement procedure risk management measures, legal aspects and the involvement of the central bank," it said.

Under EMU, the systems must uniformly ensure speedy, smooth and reliable transactions, the cross-border use of assets in the euro area, links between the ESCB and a broad range of counterparties, and the use of a wide range of eligible assets.
Harmonised working hours -- tailored to those of the TARGET gross payment system -- would also be needed, the EMI said. TARGET is set to operate from 0600 GMT to 1700 GMT.
The system must be able to handle both pledging and full transfer of eligible paper, to meet different conventions in the security of collateral at national central banks, it added.

Improved international links will be particularly important in the relatively new situation where a bank might wish to use a security deposited in another country within the euro area as collateral for loans from its domestic central bank, it said.
"The use of assets deposited in another Member State for monetary policy operations is currently rare among national central banks," the EMI said.

"Present arrangements would probably be inadequate to enable central banks' counterparties in monetary policy operations to use securities deposited in another Member State in a systematic way," it added.
Failure to achieve this could leave the euro market for short-term debt looking fragmented, it said.
The institute said it was currently examining two models to overcome this problem in the short-term, adding that implementation of a full solution by 1999 was unrealistic.
Under the first model national central banks would open accounts with one another and act a custodians for other national central banks.
Under the second system, the "foreign" national central bank holding the deposit would offer a guarantee to the home central bank of the would-be borrower.
